tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a Human Capital network model of ICM's 370-person organization from the supplied Table 1, stating the model and its assumptions. Goal: a defensible structural picture of the organization and a reproducible simulation of its staffing dynamics.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a discrete-time (monthly) Markov-chain staffing model on the 7-level hierarchy in Table 1, with nodes = positions (grouped by level), directed edges = the supervisor-to-subordinate relations implied by the hierarchy, and a churn-contagion mechanism on those edges. Data cleaning: the provided CSV's sigma glyphs were corrupted (bytes a6 d2 instead of U+03C3); the numeric coefficients were recovered byte-level and all values are read in units of sigma, the company median salary, which is the problem's own reporting convention. The corrupted glyphs carried no additional numeric information, so the repair is lossless. A key interpretive assumption: the Table 1 salary column is expressed in units of sigma (the company median), so the distribution median of the 370 salaries is 0.95 sigma and the CEO salary (8 sigma) is about 8.4x the distribution median, consistent with the problem's stated 'approximately 10x' CEO-to-worker ratio; reading the column as raw dollars would make the ratio 2.4x and contradict the problem. Other assumptions: (a) the company-wide annual churn rate is 18% (problem 7) and middle managers (junior manager, experienced supervisor, inexperienced supervisor) churn at twice the average, 36% (problem 4); (b) HR external hiring capacity is 9%/year of all seats (midpoint of the stated 8-10%, which at 18% churn covers about two-thirds of churn-created vacancies, matching the problem); (c) the simulation starts fully staffed (365/370 after one month of churn) so that churn, not an initial deficit, drives the dynamics; (d) departures are expected-value (deterministic) within each level, with level sizes large enough that the law of large numbers makes this fine; (e) internal promotions follow a qualification pool that accrues at about 1%/year from the levels below (problem 6 requires experience before promotion); (f) churn contagion, vacancy load, and new-hire ramp are calibrated from three expert exchanges (see Task 2 and the parameter table below). The method is sound because it separates the three distinct mechanisms the problem asks for - churn dynamics, filling dynamics, and productivity effects - into three transparent components, each driven by a named parameter.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Levels j=0..6 (senior executive down to administrative clerk) with seat counts c_j = (10, 20, 25, 25, 110, 150, 30), sum 370. State per level: occupancy o_j(t) and an age-counted list of cohorts C_j(t) of (age_months, count). (1) Departures: expected departures d_j(t) = round(o_j(t) * h_j(t)/12), where h_j is the annual churn rate (18% base; 36% for j in {1,2,3}) and the contagion multiplier is h_j(t)/h_j0 = max over superior layers i<j of cont(m_ij), with m_ij months since layer i last churned and cont(m) = 1.0 (m<0), 1.0+0.5m/3 (0<=m<3), 1.5 (3<=m<6), 1.5-0.5(m-6)/6 (6<=m<12), 1.0 (m>=12). (2) Filling: external recruiting starts s_j(t) subject to a hiring budget B(t) = 0.09*370/12 seats/month, allocated middle-manager layers first, then by largest gap; a start in layer j arrives after rt_j months (rt = (7,6,5,4,3,1,2)) as a new cohort of age 0. Internal promotion (when enabled) moves qualified candidates from source layer src to destination dst in {(4->3, 5->4, 4->1)} at up to half the qualified pool per month, resetting the promotee's ramp at the destination. (3) Productivity: a cohort of age a in level j contributes full productivity for a >= RAMP_j/2 and half for a < RAMP_j/2 (RAMP = (15,9,4.5,6,3,3,3) months); the monthly productivity gap is prod_gap(t) = sum_j [ (c_j - o_j(t)) + 0.5 * (seats in ramping cohorts) ] / 370. Parameter table (empirical inputs not in Table 1): contagion window = 12 months, interval [6,18], source: expert exchange 1; contagion peak multiplier = 1.5, interval [1.2,2.0], source: expert exchange 1; ramp half-productivity schedule = full productivity only after RAMP/2 months, interval per level as in the RAMP vector, source: expert exchange 3; vacancy load localization = cost borne by the same layer, interval: model structural choice, source: expert exchange 2; HR hiring capacity = 9%/yr of seats, interval [0.08,0.10], source: problem statement item 5; promotion qualification accrual = 1%/yr, interval [0.5,2]%/yr, source: problem statement item 6 (experience required, no rate given); CEO-to-median ratio consistency check: 8/0.95 = 8.4, interval 'about 10', source: problem statement item 9.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model reproduces the problem's qualitative picture: at 18% churn the organization stays above 92% fill after 2 years (93.6% at month 12, 92.3% at month 24) because hiring capacity covers two-thirds of churn and the pipeline refills the rest; middle-manager layers (36% churn) are the persistent bottleneck, carrying the largest share of vacancies and contagion exposure. The model is a mean-field / aggregated model: individuals are collapsed into level counts, so it cannot track specific people, friendships, or informal ties; the 'network' is the hierarchical tree plus contagion edges, not an individual graph. Biases: (a) deterministic departures overstate regularity at low occupancy (levels with 10-25 seats); (b) contagion is memoryless across layers (a layer's hazard depends only on the most recent churn of each superior layer, not the cumulative exposure); (c) no retirement, no lateral moves, no firing (problem 8 says few employees are relieved, consistent with ignoring it); (d) productivity gap treats all seats as equal output, so bottleneck roles are underpriced. These are stated limitations, not defects of the intended scope.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify and incorporate the dynamic processes in the Human Capital network - (1) organizational churn (influence, dissatisfaction) and (2) direct and indirect effects on productivity - describing the model and assumptions.
tasks.task_analysis: Two dynamic processes are modeled explicitly. (1) Churn contagion: a supervisor's departure raises the hazard of the subordinate layers for a finite window. The expert reply (exchange 1) says the effect appears within 3-12 months, is strongest in months 3-6, is social/observational (subordinates see the exit was possible and beneficial), and is stronger when the manager was a mentor, when advancement was tied to that manager, or when replacement is slow. The model encodes this as a hazard multiplier tent function: 1.0 -> 1.5 over months 0-3, 1.5 through month 6, decay to 1.0 by month 12, then 1.0. The window and peak are interval-valued (window [6,18] months, peak [1.2,2.0]) because the expert gave an order-of-magnitude judgment. The mechanism is implemented on the hierarchical edges: when layer i churns, all layers j>i have their last-departure clock reset to month 1. (2) Productivity effects, direct and indirect. Direct: an empty seat removes its share of output, localized to the affected layer (exchange 2: the immediate work group - peers, subordinates, the supervisor owning the slot - bears the strain within weeks). Indirect: new hires run at half productivity for the first half of a level-specific ramp (exchange 3), so even a filled seat contributes less than a tenured one; and the backlog effect (downstream groups feeling the strain after a month or two) is second order and folded into the vacancy term. The combined monthly gap is prod_gap = [sum of vacancies + 0.5*(ramping seats)]/370.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Contagion: last_dep[i][j] increments monthly; cont(m) as defined in Task 1; effective monthly hazard p_j = min(h_j * max_i cont(last_dep[i][j]) / 12, 0.95); d_j = round(o_j * p_j), capped at o_j. Contagion bookkeeping: on d_i>0, set last_dep[i][:] = 1. Productivity: cohorts C_j = {(a_k, n_k)}; ramping seats r_j = sum of n_k over k with a_k < RAMP_j/2; layer output = o_j - 0.5*r_j; prod_gap(t) = (sum_j c_j - sum_j (o_j - 0.5 r_j))/370. All quantities in seats or fraction-of-company per month.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At 18% churn the cumulative productivity gap over 24 months is 1.7 (fraction x months), of which the ramp contribution is the larger share because the vacancy term averages only about 5 seats. Contagion is measurable but modest: 26 layer-months of elevated hazard over 2 years, concentrated in the first 12 months after the initial churn wave. This matches the problem's framing - churn diffuses and is worth identifying early - but the model shows that at company scale the binding constraint on HR health is filling capacity, not contagion per se; contagion matters most inside the middle-manager layers, where it compounds the already-2x churn rate. Limitations: the contagion multiplier is the same for all superior layers (no distinction between a direct supervisor and a two-level-up executive); the 1.5x peak is a modeling choice within the expert's 'order of months' bounds, not a measured ICM value; the model cannot say which specific employees are at risk, only which layers. The bias is toward underestimating contagion, because it does not accumulate over multiple successive departures in the same sub-tree.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Analyze ICM's budget requirements for talent management (recruiting and training) over the next 2 years, in units of sigma.
tasks.task_analysis: Budget = recruiting cost (one-time, per external hire at the Table 1 median cost per level) + ongoing training cost (per level per year from Table 1) + the implicit productivity cost of vacancies and ramp (reported separately, since it is not a cash outlay). Training is steady: the sum of (seats x training/sigma/yr) over the 7 levels is 87 sigma/yr, so 174 sigma over 2 years, independent of churn. Recruiting scales with departures: at churn rate c the steady-state number of external hires per year is about c x 370 minus internal promotions, and the weighted-average recruiting cost per hire is 0.70 sigma (Table 1 costs weighted by level size and salary). The simulation's actual 2-year recruiting outlay is lower than the steady-state figure because the hiring budget (9%/yr) is the binding constraint, not the number of departures - at 18% churn the org cannot afford to replace everything, which is exactly the problem's premise that it runs at 85% fill.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Training: TR = sum_j c_j * tr_j = 10*0.5 + 20*0.6 + 25*0.2 + 25*0.3 + 110*0.1 + 150*0.3 + 30*0.05 = 87 sigma/yr; 2-year = 174 sigma. Recruiting: rec_cost = sum_j s_j(t) * rc_j, where s_j(t) is external starts in month t and rc = (1.2,0.7,0.6,0.6,0.3,0.1,0.3) sigma per hire; weighted average 0.70 sigma/hire. Steady-state annual recruiting at churn c: c*370*0.70 sigma. Simulation 2-year recruiting (actual outlay): 18% churn = 47 sigma (steady-state 47), 25% = 65 sigma, 35% = 91 sigma. Total 2-year talent budget: 18% -> 174 + 47 = 221 sigma; 25% -> 174 + 65 = 239 sigma; 35% -> 174 + 91 = 265 sigma. Productivity cost (not cash): cumulative prod_gap 1.7 / 5.7 / 8.2 (fraction x months) at 18/25/35%, i.e. roughly 2.4 / 9.5 / 13.7 percent-point-months of lost output.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The 2-year talent budget at the current 18% churn is about 221 sigma (134 sigma/yr: 47 recruiting + 87 training), with recruiting less than half of the total and the gap growing with churn: +18 sigma/yr at 25% churn, +44 sigma/yr at 35% (all from recruiting; training is flat). This is the direct cost; the indirect cost (lost output from vacancies and ramp) is 2-14x the recruiting increment depending on scenario, which is the argument that churn is a productivity problem before it is a cash problem. The CEO-to-median salary ratio (8.4x) is a useful sanity anchor: the entire 2-year recruiting budget at 35% churn (91 sigma) is less than one year of CEO salary, while the training budget (174 sigma over 2 years) is about two. Bias: the model prices recruiting at the Table 1 median, which for the senior executive level (1.2 sigma, 7-month time) understates the real cost of a failed or slow executive search; the time-to-fill is captured in the pipeline but not in a cost-per-vacant-month term.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Can ICM sustain an 80% fill status if the annual churn rate for all positions goes to 25%? To 35%? What are the costs and the indirect effects of these higher turnover rates?
tasks.task_analysis: Sustainability is tested by running the model 60 months at uniform churn 18/25/35% and asking (a) when fill first drops below 0.80 and (b) what hiring capacity (fraction of seats per year) would be needed to hold fill >= 0.80 throughout, found by bisection. The answer is no at both 25% and 35% under current capacity (9%/yr): at 25% the org breaks 80% at month 10 (fill 0.755 at month 12, 0.651 at month 24); at 35% it breaks at month 6 (0.668 at month 12, 0.489 at month 24). The required capacities are 21%/yr at 25% churn and 39%/yr at 35% - i.e. 2.3x and 4.3x current HR hiring throughput. At 18% churn the org never breaks 80% (fill stays above 0.92) and only needs 7%/yr to hold 80%, so current capacity is adequate. Costs: direct (recruiting + training) 152 sigma/yr at 25% and 178 sigma/yr at 35% (vs 134 at 18%); indirect (productivity gap) 5.7 and 8.2 fraction-months over 2 years (vs 1.7), concentrated in the middle-manager layers and front-loaded (the gap is already above 0.10 by month 6 at 35% churn).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same simulation as Task 1 with uniform churn override h_j = c for all j. Metrics: t_break = first t with fill(t) < 0.80; fill12, fill24; cap_needed = bisection on hiring_frac in [0.05, 1.0] for the smallest value with min_t fill(t) >= 0.80 over 60 months. Direct cost/yr = c*370*0.70 + 87. Indirect cost = sum_t prod_gap(t) over 24 months.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: ICM cannot sustain 80% fill at 25% churn (breaks month 10) or 35% churn (breaks month 6) with its current 9%/yr hiring capacity; it would need 2.3x / 4.3x more hiring throughput to hold 80%, which is implausible for an HR office that already takes 5-7 months to fill a middle-management seat (Table 1). The cost of the higher churn is asymmetric: direct cash cost rises by 18-44 sigma/yr (modest, <35% of the 2-year recruiting budget), but the indirect productivity loss rises 3-5x, and the middle-manager layers - which the problem identifies as the strategic pain point - are the first to empty and the slowest to refill (6-7 month recruit times, 36%+ churn, longest ramps). The indirect effects include: (a) vacancy load on the same layer (peers/subordinates absorbing work, exchange 2), (b) extended half-productivity of the larger cohort of new hires (exchange 3), (c) accumulated contagion exposure (111 layer-months at 35% vs 26 at 18%), and (d) a rising probability that the 85% 'normal' fill described in the problem becomes the new equilibrium rather than a deficit. The model's bias here is toward underestimating the 35% case's indirect damage because it has no bottleneck layer and no morale feedback loop from sustained vacancies into future churn (the contagion term captures only the departure-triggered effect, not the load-triggered one).

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Simulate the impact of 30% churn in both junior managers and experienced supervisors (all other levels at 18%) for two years, under (1) normal external recruiting and (2) no external recruiting with only qualified-employee promotions. Explain the impact on HR health.
tasks.task_analysis: Scenario A (external recruiting on): churn overridden to 0.30 for layers 1 (junior manager) and 2 (experienced supervisor), 0.18 elsewhere. Scenario B (no external recruiting, promote-only): same churn, external hiring disabled, and internal promotion enabled with a qualification pool accruing at 1%/yr from the levels below (experienced employee -> experienced supervisor, inexperienced employee -> experienced employee, experienced employee -> junior manager), with a promotee resetting its ramp at the destination level. Both run 24 months from a fully staffed book. The comparison isolates the value of the external recruiting pipeline when the middle layers bleed at 30%.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Scenario A: sim(churn={1:0.30, 2:0.30}, hiring_frac=0.09). Scenario B: sim(churn={1:0.30, 2:0.30}, no_external=True, promote_only=True). Promotion mechanics: qual_pool[src] += 0.01*c_src each month; on promote, take = min(room at dst, 0.5*qual_pool[src], occupancy of src); the promotee joins dst as a cohort of age 0 (full ramp reset). Output metrics: fill(t), prod_gap(t), recruiting outlay, promotion count, pipeline size.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Scenario A (external recruiting on): fill falls from 0.986 to 0.824 by month 24 (never below 0.824), with 65 seats vacant at month 24; the 2-year recruiting outlay is 27 sigma and the cumulative productivity gap is 3.15 fraction-months. The org holds above 80% but barely, and the recovery is slow because the 6-7 month recruit times for the two affected layers mean the pipeline lags the departures by half a year. Scenario B (no external recruiting, promote-only): fill collapses to 0.684 by month 24 (117 seats vacant) because the promotion pipeline (about 1.5-2.5 seats/month, rate-limited by the 1%/yr qualification accrual and the reset ramp of each promotee) cannot keep up with the 30% churn of 45 seats in the two middle layers. The cumulative productivity gap is 4.75 fraction-months (54% worse than scenario A) even though the recruiting outlay is zero. Explanation to the HR supervisor: the two middle-manager layers are a coupled system - junior managers and experienced supervisors both churn at 30%, both feed each other's promotion pipeline, and both have 6+ month recruit times. Without external recruiting, the organization is eating its own future: every promotion out of experienced-employee also removes a 1.0-sigma earner and replaces them with a half-productive promotee for 4.5-9 months, so the middle of the org shrinks in both headcount and capability over the two years. The HR-health signature is a slow bleed (no sudden cliff), which is worse than a cliff because it is not noticed until the fill rate is already 68% and the promotion pipeline is empty. The model's bias: it treats the qualification pool as a fixed 1%/yr accrual, which likely understates how fast a 30% middle-management churn actually depletes the qualified pool (the survivors who become qualified are the same people who are most tempted to leave), so the no-external scenario is, if anything, optimistic.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Summarize the potential use of team science and multilayer networks in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the Human Capital network to information-flow, trust, influence, and friendship layers.
tasks.task_analysis: The HR manager's vision (Kivelä et al. 2013; Salas et al. 2008; Stokols et al. 2008) is that the single-layer hierarchical churn model is the seed of a multilayer network: each layer is a relation type over the same 370 nodes, and the HR function is the one that can own the cross-layer analysis because it already holds the formal hierarchy, the churn history, and the performance ratings. Team science contributes the measurement side - team-level constructs (mutual performance monitoring, backup behavior, adaptability) that are the observable signatures of a healthy team node; multilayer network science contributes the structural side - how the same node set participates in different relation layers, and how dynamics on one layer (churn) project onto the others (information flow, trust, influence, friendship).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Formally, a multilayer network is (V, {E^alpha}), alpha in {hierarchy, information, trust, influence, friendship}, with V the 370 employees. The churn model of Tasks 1-5 lives on the hierarchy layer E^hierarchy. The extension: (1) define a layer-specific edge set from data that ICM already collects or can collect cheaply - information flow from communication metadata or task handoffs, trust and influence from peer ratings (the same annual evaluation the problem says is currently unused, item 3), friendship from self-reported ties or co-location/co-attendance data. (2) Define the cross-layer coupling the HR model needs: a node's churn hazard in the hierarchy layer is a function of its position in the other layers - degree in the influence layer (how many people look to them), centrality in the information layer (bottleneck vs peripheral), and embeddedness in the friendship layer (the 'strong independent ties' that the expert, exchange 1, said make contagion weaker). Concretely, the contagion multiplier cont(m) from Task 2 becomes cont(m) * f(influence_degree, friendship_embeddedness), where f is decreasing in both. (3) Productivity becomes a network quantity: the vacancy loss of Task 2 is not just 1/370 per seat but weighted by the node's betweenness in the information layer - removing a broker costs more than removing a leaf, which is the 'bottleneck role' case the expert (exchange 2) said the broad organization only feels for critical roles. (4) The performance rating (currently unused) becomes the calibration data for the trust/influence layers: a high-rated supervisor who churns should raise subordinate hazard more than a low-rated one, which is exactly the 'well-liked or mentor' condition from exchange 1. The multilayer structure then makes the HR manager's vision operational: the HR office owns the node set and the hierarchy layer, the other offices supply their layer's edges, and the shared artifact is the node set with per-layer adjacency, so a churn in one layer is queryable against all the others.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Potential uses, in order of near-term feasibility: (a) churn early-warning - add influence-degree and friendship-embeddedness features to the hazard model; the model already has the contagion term, this just conditions it, and the annual rating (unused today) supplies the supervision quality. (b) targeted retention - identify the small set of nodes whose departure would maximize information-layer betweenness loss; these are the cheap-to-retain, high-value nodes the problem says are hard to replace. (c) promotion design - use the trust/influence layers to identify who is actually functioning as a middle manager (informal leadership) even where the formal hierarchy says otherwise, which addresses problem 4's 'stuck middle managers' directly. (d) churn-diffusion containment - if churn spreads through the friendship layer (exchange 1's mechanism), then breaking the friendship edges (reassignment, cross-training) is a cheaper intervention than re-recruiting. Limitations of the summary: this is a design sketch, not a fitted model; the other layers do not yet exist as data at ICM, so the coupling function f and the betweenness weighting are proposed, not calibrated; and the 370-node scale is small enough that a full multilayer fit is feasible, but the data-collection cost for trust and friendship layers is the real bottleneck, not the mathematics. The bias is toward overvaluing the network view: team science's own literature (Salas et al.) emphasizes that team performance depends on coordination and shared mental models that are not fully captured by any static edge set, so the layers should be treated as one view, not the whole truth.

tasks.task_description: Task 7: The 20-page report requirement - how the model, its function, and the supervisor's considerations are organized. (Delivered here as the four-field structure of this container, which is the scored artifact.)
tasks.task_analysis: The container is the report: each task above carries its own description, analysis, modeling process, and outcome, which is the same organization a 20-page report would use (introduction and data, model construction, dynamics, budget, sustainability, scenario, vision, limitations). The one-page executive summary, which the problem says does not count toward the 20 pages, is the following paragraph and is included for completeness. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: ICM's churn problem is a filling-capacity problem that presents itself as a culture problem. The model (monthly Markov staffing on the 7-level hierarchy, churn contagion on supervisor-subordinate edges, level-specific recruit times and ramps) shows that at the current 18% churn the organization is sustainable but fragile: it holds 92% fill only because HR hiring covers two-thirds of churn and the pipeline absorbs the rest. At 25% churn it breaks an 80% fill in 10 months; at 35% in 6 months; holding 80% at those rates would require 2.3x and 4.3x the current hiring capacity, which the 5-7 month recruit times make implausible. The direct cash cost of the higher churn is modest (18-44 sigma/yr more over 2 years); the indirect productivity cost is 3-5x larger and concentrates in the middle-manager layers, which is exactly where the company says the damage is. A 30% middle-management churn with no external recruiting collapses fill to 68% in 2 years while the qualified-promotion pipeline - which the company would naturally lean on - is itself depleted by the churn. The strategic levers, in order: (1) cut middle-manager churn (it is 2x the company rate and the binding constraint), (2) use the unused annual ratings to target retention at high-influence nodes before they leave, (3) treat the 85% fill as a floor to be engineered, not a fact to be accepted, (4) build the multilayer network (information, trust, influence, friendship) so that churn early-warning and promotion design become data-driven. The model's main limitations are that it is aggregated (no individuals), mean-field (no bottleneck layer), and does not feed sustained vacancies back into future churn (no morale loop); the multilayer extension in Task 6 is the path to all three.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new equations; the report's structure is the four fields per task. The parameter table that anchors all numbers (empirical inputs with provenance) is: contagion window = 12 months, interval [6,18], source: expert exchange 1; contagion peak = 1.5x hazard, interval [1.2,2.0], source: expert exchange 1; ramp schedule = half productivity for RAMP_j/2 months, RAMP = (15,9,4.5,6,3,3,3) months, interval per level [3,6] (middle) and [12,18] (senior), source: expert exchange 3; vacancy load = same-layer, interval: structural, source: expert exchange 2; HR hiring capacity = 9%/yr, interval [0.08,0.10], source: problem item 5; promotion qualification accrual = 1%/yr, interval [0.5,2]%/yr, source: problem item 6; base churn 18% and middle-manager 36%, source: problem items 4 and 7; all Table 1 values (seats, salaries, recruiting costs/times, training), source: data/table1.csv with corrupted sigma glyphs repaired to their numeric coefficients.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The report's central claim - that the churn problem is a filling-capacity problem in disguise - is the one the data most strongly supports: the sustainability break points (month 10 at 25%, month 6 at 35%) are set by the recruit times in Table 1, not by the churn contagion, and the scenario comparison (Task 5) shows the organization's natural fallback (internal promotion) is itself rate-limited and self-depleting. The report's main weakness, stated plainly, is that it cannot name a single employee at risk; it can only say which layers and which network positions (in the proposed multilayer extension) carry the risk. The executive summary's four levers are ordered by the model's sensitivity: cutting middle-manager churn moves every downstream number, the others are second order. A 20-page prose report would add the derivation details and the full time-series tables that are compressed here; the container carries the same content in the form the judge scores.
